figures.caption: Fig. 1: Diagram of an ultra-low-power CMOS analog spiking neuron based on a simplified Morris-Lecar model [4]. The input is the excitatory current iex, while the output is the node voltage vGK.

Fig. 2: Reliability of spike timing in a rat neocortical neuron stimulated by (A) a constant supra-threshold current pulse; (B) a time-varying current (frozen filtered white Gaussian noise added to a constant component). Raster plots of the spike times for 25 consecutive trials are depicted at the bottom, for both experiments. Reprinted from [12] with permission from the AAAS.

Fig. 3: CMOS analog neuron in oscillatory regime under a constant excitation current pulse of supra-threshold amplitude 20 pA. (a) Output spikes. (b) Input excitation current iex(t). (c) Raster plot of the spike times. Simulation parameters: time step ∆t = 1ns, intrinsic transistor noise bandwidth fmax = 500MHz. 1000 trials were performed; only 25 are shown.

Fig. 4: CMOS analog neuron excited by frozen filtered white Gaussian noise, fluctuation around a constant current pulse of sub-threshold amplitude 5 pA. Input noise parameters: standard deviation σiex = 20 pA, filter time constant τ = 5 µs. (a) Output spikes. (b) Input excitation current iex(t). (c) Raster plot of the spike times. Same simulation parameters as in Figure 3.

Fig. 5: Analysis of the trial-to-trial variability in the spike times for the two types of input current, respectively triggering the oscillatory (Figure 3, with mean inter-spike interval or spike period E{Tn − Tn−1} ≈ 32 µs) and excitability (Figure 4) behaviours. The jitter only accumulates over time for the former. The variance was estimated from 1000 trials. As discussed in the text, the variances of the 4th and 15th spike times of Figure 4 are very large (20 and 8 (µs)2) and go off the scale of the plot.
